contexts.value: Farm-level mitigation strategies with potential to minimise life cycle GHG emissions were placed in the context of the cradle-to-gate system to account for associated changes in pre-farm and post-farm emissions
contexts.original_text: Farm level management options with potential to minimise life cycle GHG emissions were: reducing N fertiliser rate from a commercial rate of 255 kg N/ha to 240 kg N/ha or 180 kg N/ha (2.6% and 13.2% emissions reduction); use of controlled-release and stabilised N fertilisers (5.9% reduction), changing from diesel to solar-powered irrigation pumps (8.1% reduction), changing from diesel to biofuel-powered farm machinery (3.4% reduction), changing from continuous cotton to a cotton-legume crop rotation (3.9% reduction) and use of N fertigation (2.1% reduction). Whilst we focused on farm-level mitigation strategies, these changes were placed in the context of the cradle-to-gate system, to account for associated changes in pre-farm and post-farm emissions.

contexts.value: Opportunities to sequester carbon were not included due to uncertainties

contexts.value: Focused on Namoi and Gwydir regions in northwest NSW as this area is strongly representative of Australian cotton production
contexts.original_text: We chose to focus on the Namoi and Gwydir regions in northwest NSW, as production in this area is strongly representative of Australian cotton production (Hedayati, 2015).

contexts.value: Limited study to climate change impact of cotton production on GHG emissions
contexts.original_text: Whilst Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) can be applied across a broad array of impact categories, we limited this study to the climate change impact of cotton production on GHG emissions.

contexts.original_text: The geographical scope of the LCA was the cotton growing region of northwest NSW Australia, in the Namoi-Gwydir regions including the towns of Narrabri, Moree and Walgett.

contexts.value: The towns of Narrabri, Moree and Walgett in the cotton-growing Namoi-Gwydir regions of northwest NSW.
contexts.original_text: The geographical scope of the LCA was the cotton growing region of northwest NSW Australia, in the Namoi-Gwydir regions including the towns of Narrabri, Moree and Walgett.

contexts.value: 3 production seasons
contexts.original_text: The temporal scope of the LCA was the three cotton production seasons of 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014.
The temporal scope of the LCA was the three cotton production seasons of 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014.

contexts.value: The system boundary of the LCA study included the pre-farm, on-farm and post-farm stages to provide an understanding of the full life cycle consequences of practice changes in these stages.
contexts.original_text: The system boundary of the LCA study (Fig. 1) included the prefarm stage (i.e. production and transport of raw materials), the onfarm stage (i.e. cotton farming practices) and the post-farm stage (i.e. cotton ginning and the transport of cotton lint to an export port). This approach provided an understanding of the full life cycle consequences of pre-farm, on-farm and post-farm practice changes.

contexts.value: 80% of irrigation water sourced from surface water versus 20% from groundwater.
contexts.original_text: The percentage of irrigation water sourced from surface water (80%) versus groundwater (20%) assumed for this study is based on the percentage reported for extractive agricultural use in NSW in 2012-2013 (ABS, 2014).

contexts.value: 85% of irrigation water pumped by diesel-powered irrigation pumps and 15% by electric pumps.
contexts.original_text: We assumed that 85% of the irrigation water was pumped by diesel-powered irrigation pumps and 15% by electric pumps (Foley et al., 2015).

contexts.value: Total dynamic heads for water pumped from surface water assumed to be 8m.
contexts.original_text: The total dynamic heads for water pumped from surface water and groundwater were assumed to be 8 m (Welke, 2011) and 35 m (NSW Water, 2009a; b), respectively.

contexts.value: Total dynamic heads for water pumped from ground water assumed to be 35m.
contexts.original_text: The total dynamic heads for water pumped from surface water and groundwater were assumed to be 8 m (Welke, 2011) and 35 m (NSW Water, 2009a; b), respectively.

contexts.value: Applied the relative contributions of cotton lint, cottonseed, and gin trash for a typical Australian ginning plant
contexts.original_text: We applied the relative contributions of cotton lint (42%), cottonseed (49%) and gin trash (9%) for a typical Australian ginning plant (RIRDC, 2014).

contexts.value: Process flows with a cumulative mass or energy of less than 1% were excluded
contexts.original_text: All process flows with a cumulative mass or energy of less than 1% were excluded, e.g. packaging glues used at the cotton gin.

contexts.value: N fertiliser application rate was modified from a commercial rate (255 kg N/ha) to the rate at which lint yield is reported to be maximised (240 kg N/ha) and also to the economically optimum rate (180 kg N/ha).
contexts.original_text: When assessing mitigation options, the N fertiliser application rate was modified from a commercial rate of 255 kg N/ha to 240 kg N/ha, the rate at which lint yield is reported to be maximised (Macdonald et al., 2015), and also to 180 kg N/ha, the economically optimum rate according to Visser et al. (2015).

contexts.value: Controlled release and stabilised fertilisers were included in the analysis.
contexts.original_text: The controlled release (polymer-coated urea) and stabilised fertilisers (urea treated with a nitrification inhibitor) were included in the analysis.

contexts.value: Applied a 52% reduction in each emissions factor during the on-farm phase.
contexts.original_text: We applied a 52% reduction in each emissions factor during the onfarm phase, as per Tian et al. (2015). The increase in fertiliser manufacturing emissions required to produce these products was negligible and below the 1% cut-off for inclusion in the LCA.

contexts.value: Fertigation was assessed as a mitigation strategy by removing the pre-plant fertiliser operation and reducing the N2O produced from applied N by 80%.
contexts.original_text: The use of fertigation as a mitigation strategy was assessed by removing the pre-plant fertiliser operation and reducing the N2O produced from applied N by 80% (Antille, 2018).

contexts.value: Chickpea was modelled to represent a typical legume crop grown in rotation with cotton.
contexts.original_text: Chickpea was modelled as a surrogate representing a typical legume crop grown in rotation with cotton, given the ready availability of data on emissions from chickpea production specific to northwest NSW.

contexts.value: Did not credit the cotton with the N fixed during growth of the chickpea crop, instead applied a yield increase to account for break-crop effects.
contexts.original_text: For the purpose of this study, we did not credit the cotton with the N fixed during growth of the chickpea crop, instead applying a yield increase to account for break-crop effects.

contexts.value: Did not debit the system with carbon sequestration during legume production due to low biomass of legume crops.
contexts.original_text: Also, we did not debit the system with the foregone carbon sequestration that occurs during legume production due to the lower biomass of legume crops.

contexts.value: 3 kW solar panels assumed to be the power source for solar-powered irrigation pumps.
contexts.original_text: For solar-powered irrigation pumps, 3 kW solar panels were assumed as the power source.

contexts.value: Biodiesel produced as methyl ester from rapeseed assumed to be the fuel for biofuel-powered farm machinery.
contexts.original_text: For biofuel-powered farm machinery, biodiesel was assumed to be produced as methyl ester from rapeseed, with the CO2 emissions from the combustion of biodiesel considered biogenic and thus not included in the impact assessment.

contexts.value: CO2 emissions from the combustion of biodiesel considered biogenic and thus not included in the impact assessment.
contexts.original_text: For biofuel-powered farm machinery, biodiesel was assumed to be produced as methyl ester from rapeseed, with the CO2 emissions from the combustion of biodiesel considered biogenic and thus not included in the impact assessment.

contexts.original_text: The economic analysis data was based on Powell and Scott (2011). We applied the most representative, rather than average yield data.

contexts.value: Global warming potentials (GWPs) applied for CO2, N2O, and CH4 were 1, 298, and 25, respectively.
contexts.original_text: The global warming potentials (GWPs) applied for CO2, N2O, and CH4 were 1, 298, and 25, respectively (Australian Government, 2015a).

contexts.value: CO2 absorbed by the cotton crop during its growth and the CO2 released from the decomposition of cotton residues in the field were excluded from the primary LCA.
contexts.original_text: As the NIR methods do not include CH4 emissions on-farm, CH4 is only reported as a component of pre-farm processes, where it is expressed in CO2-equivalents (CO2e). For consistency with these guidelines, we excluded CO2 absorbed by the cotton crop during its growth and the CO2 released from the decomposition of cotton residues in the field (i.e. biogenic CO2) from the primary LCA.

contexts.value: External data was used to calculate fertiliser-related emissions and emissions from the decomposition of cotton residues.
contexts.original_text: We drew data from an Australian cotton-related publication (Australian Government, 2015b) when calculating fertiliser-related emissions and accessed data from Muhammad (2011) when calculating emissions from the decomposition of cotton residues.

contexts.original_text: We applied an average cotton lint price from 2011 to 2014 of $2070/t ($470/bale) and average cottonseed price of $300/t, allocating approximately 86% of the life cycle climate change impact to lint.

contexts.original_text: So, we applied a fraction of 20% of cottonseed as animal feed and then conducted sensitivity testing to determine the effect of this assumption.

contexts.value: Extrapolated the results for northwest New South Wales to other regions due to the gap in knowledge about the greenhouse gas emissions intensity associated with Australian cotton production.
contexts.original_text: Given the gap in knowledge about the greenhouse gas emissions intensity associated with Australian cotton production, we extrapolated the results for northwest New South Wales to other regions and tested the sensitivity of the emissions profile to our given system assumptions.

contexts.original_text: Whilst we accounted for lower N fertiliser requirements in dryland systems, we did not adjust emissions factors for lower soil moisture, given the small contribution of dryland cotton (4%) to overall production volumes.
